blocks.p: By this time they had come to the Enchanted Ground, where the very air tends to make a person drowsy. The whole place was overgrown with briars and thorns, except here and there where an enchanted arbor stood; and if a man sits down in one of those, or sleeps in one, it is a question, some say, whether he will ever rise or wake again in this world. So over this forest they went, every one of them, Mr. Great-heart in front, since he was the guide, and Mr. Valiant-for-truth behind as a rear guard, in case some fiend or dragon or giant or thief should fall on them from behind and do them harm. They went on here each with his sword drawn in his hand, for they knew it was a dangerous place; and they cheered one another along as well as they could. Mr. Great-heart ordered Feeble-mind to come up right behind him, and Mr. Despondency was kept under the eye of Mr. Valiant.

They had not gone far when a great mist and darkness fell on them all, so that for a long while they could hardly see one another, and for some time they had to feel for each other with words; for they did not walk by sight.

Anyone can imagine that this was sorry going for the best of them; but how much worse for the women and children, who were tender both in feet and in heart. Yet through the encouraging words of the one who led in front and the one who brought up the rear, they managed to keep plodding along.

The way here was also very wearisome, through dirt and slime. And on all this ground there was not a single inn or eating house where the feebler ones could be refreshed. So here there was grunting and puffing and sighing. While one tumbled over a bush, another stuck fast in the mud; and some of the children lost their shoes in the mire. One cried out, “I’m down!” and another, “Hey! Where are you?” and a third, “The bushes have got such a grip on me, I don’t think I can get free of them.”

Then they came to an arbor, warm and promising rich refreshment to pilgrims; for it was finely built overhead, decorated with greenery, and furnished with benches and seats. It also had in it a soft couch where the weary might lie down. All things considered, you may be sure this was tempting, for the pilgrims were already beginning to be worn down by the badness of the way; yet not one of them made so much as a motion to stop there. In fact, as far as I could see, they paid such close attention to their guide’s advice, and he warned them so faithfully of dangers, and of the nature of dangers, as they came to them, that usually, when they were nearest to danger, they most plucked up their spirits and heartened one another to deny the flesh. This arbor was called the Slothful’s Friend, built on purpose to lure some of the pilgrims, if it could, to take their rest there when they were weary.

Then I saw in my dream that they went on through this lonely ground until they came to a place where a man is apt to lose his way. Now when it was light, their guide could tell well enough how to avoid the wrong turnings; but in the dark he was brought to a stand. But he had in his pocket a map of all the ways leading to and from the Celestial City. So he struck a light, for he never goes anywhere without his tinderbox either, and studied his book, or map, which told him to be careful in that place to take the right-hand way. And if he had not been careful to look at his map here, in all likelihood they would all have been smothered in mud; for just a little ahead of them, and at the end of the cleanest-looking path too, was a pit, no one knows how deep, full of nothing but mud, made there on purpose to destroy pilgrims.
Then I thought to myself: who, going on pilgrimage, would not want one of these maps with him, so that when he is brought to a stand he can look and see which way he must take?

They went on, then, through the Enchanted Ground until they came to another arbor, this one built right beside the highway. In that arbor lay two men, whose names were Heedless and Too-bold. These two had come this far on pilgrimage; but here, worn out by their journey, they had sat down to rest and had fallen fast asleep. When the pilgrims saw them, they stood still and shook their heads, for they knew the sleepers were in a pitiful state. Then they consulted about what to do: whether to go on and leave them to their sleep, or to go over and try to wake them. They decided to go to them and wake them, if they could, but with this caution: to take care not to sit down themselves or accept the offered comfort of that arbor.
So they went in and spoke to the men, calling each by name, for it seems the guide knew them; but there was no voice and no answer. Then the guide shook them and did what he could to rouse them.
“I’ll pay you when I get my money,” said one of them. At that the guide shook his head.
“I’ll fight as long as I can hold my sword in my hand,” said the other. At that one of the children laughed.
“What is the meaning of this?” said Christiana.

“They are talking in their sleep,” said the guide. “Strike them, beat them, do whatever you like to them, they will answer you like this; or as one of them said in old times, when the waves of the sea were beating on him and he slept like a man on the mast of a ship, ‘When shall I awake? I will seek it yet again.’ [Prov. 23:34-35] You know that when men talk in their sleep they say anything; their words are governed neither by faith nor by reason. There is an incoherence in their words now, just as there was before, between their going on pilgrimage and their sitting down here. This, then, is the mischief of it: when heedless people go on pilgrimage, it is twenty to one that they end up like this. For this Enchanted Ground is one of the last refuges the enemy of pilgrims has; and that is why, as you see, it is placed almost at the end of the way, where it stands against us with the greater advantage. For when, thinks the enemy, will these fools be so eager to sit down as when they are weary? And when are they so likely to be weary as when they are almost at their journey’s end? That is why, I say, the Enchanted Ground is placed so near the Land of Beulah, and so near the end of their race. So let pilgrims look to themselves, in case it happens to them as it has to these two, who, as you see, have fallen asleep, and no one can wake them.”

Then the pilgrims, trembling, wanted to go forward; only they begged their guide to strike a light, so that they could go the rest of the way by the help of a lantern. So he struck a light, and by the help of it they went through the rest of that way, though the darkness was very great. [2 Pet. 1:19]

But the children began to be sorely weary, and they cried out to Him who loves pilgrims to make their way more comfortable. So when they had gone a little farther, a wind rose that drove away the fog, and the air became clearer. They were still not off the Enchanted Ground by much; but now they could see one another better, and the way they were to walk.

Now when they were almost at the end of this ground, they heard, a little ahead of them, the solemn sound of someone in great earnest. So they went on and looked ahead; and there they saw what seemed to be a man on his knees, with hands and eyes lifted up, speaking, as it seemed, earnestly to One above. They drew near but could not make out what he said. So they went quietly until he had finished. When he had finished, he got up and began to run toward the Celestial City.
Then Mr. Great-heart called after him: “Hello there, friend! Let us have your company, if you are going, as I suppose you are, to the Celestial City.”
So the man stopped, and they came up to him. As soon as Mr. Honest saw him, he said, “I know this man.”
“Who is it, then?” said Mr. Valiant-for-truth.
“He comes from near where I used to live. His name is Stand-fast; he is certainly a right good pilgrim.”
So they came up to one another, and at once Stand-fast said to old Honest, “Ho, Father Honest, is that you?”
“Yes, it is,” said he, “as sure as that is you.”
“I’m very glad to have found you on this road,” said Mr. Stand-fast.
“And I’m as glad that I caught sight of you on your knees,” said the other.
Then Mr. Stand-fast blushed. “What? Did you see me?”
“Yes, I did, and my heart was glad at the sight.”
“Why, what did you think?” said Stand-fast.
“Think!” said old Honest. “What should I think? I thought we had an honest man on the road, and so we should have his company before long.”
“If you thought nothing worse,” said Stand-fast, “then how happy I am; but if I am not what I should be, I alone must bear it.”
“That is true,” said the other. “But your fear only confirms me further that things are right between the Prince of Pilgrims and your soul; for he says, ‘Blessed is the man who fears always.’”
“Well, brother,” said Valiant, “tell us, what was it that had you on your knees just now? Was it that some special mercies had laid an obligation on you, or what?”

“Why, we are on the Enchanted Ground, as you see,” said Stand-fast; “and as I was coming along, I was thinking to myself what a dangerous road the road through this place is, and how many who had come even this far on pilgrimage had been stopped here and destroyed. I thought, too, of the kind of death this place destroys men with. Those who die here die of no violent disease. The death they die is not painful to them; for the man who goes away in a sleep begins that journey with desire and pleasure, and in fact gives in to the will of that disease.”
“Did you see the two men asleep in the arbor?” said Mr. Honest, interrupting him.

“Yes, yes, I saw Heedless and Too-bold there; and for all I know, there they will lie until they rot. [Prov. 10:7] But let me go on with my story. As I was thinking these things, as I said, a woman presented herself to me, very pleasantly dressed but old, and she offered me three things: her body, her purse, and her bed. Now the truth is, I was both weary and sleepy; I am also as poor as an owl, and perhaps the witch knew it. Well, I repulsed her once and twice, but she brushed my refusals aside and smiled. Then I began to get angry, but that meant nothing at all to her. Then she made her offers again, and said that if I would be ruled by her, she would make me great and happy; ‘for,’ she said, ‘I am the mistress of the world, and men are made happy by me.’ Then I asked her name, and she told me it was Madam Bubble. That set me further from her still; but she kept after me with her enticements. Then I went down on my knees, as you saw, and with hands lifted up and cries I prayed to Him who has said he will help. So just as you came up, the gentlewoman went her way. Then I went on giving thanks for my great deliverance; for I truly believe she meant me no good, but was trying to stop me on my journey.”
“Without doubt her designs were bad,” said Honest. “But wait. Now that you speak of her, I think I have either seen her or read some account of her.”
“Perhaps you have done both.”
“Madam Bubble! Isn’t she a tall, handsome woman, rather dark in complexion?”
“Right, you’ve hit it; she is just such a one.”
“Doesn’t she speak very smoothly, and give you a smile at the end of every sentence?”
“You’ve hit it again, for those are exactly her ways.”
“Doesn’t she wear a great purse at her side, and isn’t her hand often in it, fingering her money, as if that were her heart’s delight?”
“Just so. If she had stood here all this while, you could not have set her before me more fully, or described her features better.”
“Then the man who drew her picture was a good painter, and the man who wrote of her told the truth.”

“This woman is a witch,” said Mr. Great-heart, “and it is by her sorceries that this ground is enchanted. Whoever lays his head in her lap might as well lay it on the block under the hanging axe; and whoever sets his eyes on her beauty is counted an enemy of God. [James 4:4; 1 John 2:15] This is the woman who keeps all the enemies of pilgrims in their splendor. Yes, this is the one who has bought off many a man from a pilgrim’s life. She is a great gossip; she and her daughters are always at the heels of one pilgrim or another, now praising and now pressing on them the excellencies of this life. She is bold and shameless; she will talk with any man. She always laughs poor pilgrims to scorn, but she speaks highly of the rich. If there is anyone in a place who is clever at getting money, she will speak well of him from house to house. She dearly loves banqueting and feasting; she is always at one full table or another. In some places she has let it be known that she is a goddess, and so some people worship her. She has her set times and public places for cheating; and she will say, and swear to it, that no one can show a good to compare with hers. She promises to live with men’s children’s children, if they will only love her and make much of her. In some places, and to some people, she will pour gold out of her purse like dust. She loves to be sought after, to be spoken well of, and to lie in the arms of men. She never tires of praising her goods, and she loves best those who think best of her. She will promise crowns and kingdoms to some, if they will only take her advice; yet many she has brought to the gallows, and ten thousand times more to hell.”
“Oh,” said Stand-fast, “what a mercy it is that I resisted! For where might she have drawn me?”

“Where! No, none but God knows where. But in general, you can be sure, she would have drawn you into ‘many foolish and harmful desires, which drown men in destruction and ruin.’ [1 Tim. 6:9] It was she who set Absalom against his father, and Jeroboam against his master. It was she who persuaded Judas to sell his Lord, and who got Demas to abandon the godly pilgrims’ life. No one can tell all the mischief she does. She sets rulers against subjects, parents against children, neighbor against neighbor, a man against his wife, a man against himself, the flesh against the heart. So, good Master Stand-fast, be what your name says you are; and ‘when you have done all, stand.’”
At this talk there was a mixture of joy and trembling among the pilgrims; but at last they broke out and sang:
